title: 07 — Iceberg REST Catalogs
html:
07 — Iceberg REST Catalogs

The one idea: the catalog is the one component every engine must agree on. The Iceberg REST catalog specification turns it into a plain HTTP API, so Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, PyIceberg and commercial warehouses can all share tables through one server — which also becomes the single place to enforce permissions and hand out storage credentials.

1. What a catalog does

Responsibility Detail
Naming warehouse.namespace.table → current metadata file location
Atomic commit Compare-and-swap of that location; the only serialisation point in Iceberg
Namespaces Hierarchy for organising tables (bronze, silver, gold, or by domain)
Access control Who can read, write, create or drop which namespace/table
Credential vending Hands the engine short-lived, table-scoped storage credentials, so engines never hold bucket keys
Server-side features Some catalogs add table maintenance, metrics, lineage, multi-table transactions

Before the REST spec, each catalog type (Hive Metastore, AWS Glue, JDBC, Nessie) needed a client library in every engine. Now an engine implements one HTTP client and talks to any compliant server.

2. The REST catalog protocol

Main endpoints (prefix configurable, usually /v1/{prefix}/…):

Call Endpoint
Discover settings GET /v1/config?warehouse=demo
List / create namespaces GET, POST /v1/{prefix}/namespaces
List / create tables GET, POST /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{ns}/tables
Load table GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{ns}/tables/{table} → metadata + optional credentials
Commit POST /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{ns}/tables/{table} with requirements and updates
Multi-table commit POST /v1/{prefix}/transactions/commit
Views …/views endpoints

A commit request says what must still be true and what to change:

{
  "requirements": [
    { "type": "assert-table-uuid", "uuid": "5d1c…" },
    { "type": "assert-ref-snapshot-id", "ref": "main", "snapshot-id": 6114 }
  ],
  "updates": [
    { "action": "add-snapshot", "snapshot": { "snapshot-id": 7311, "parent-snapshot-id": 6114, … } },
    { "action": "set-snapshot-ref", "ref-name": "main", "type": "branch", "snapshot-id": 7311 }
  ]
}

If main is no longer at 6114, the server returns 409 Conflict and the client reloads and retries. This is how optimistic concurrency works over HTTP.

Authentication is typically OAuth2 (client credentials or token exchange) or a bearer token, configured in the engine.

3. The main open implementations

Catalog Notes
Lakekeeper Rust, Apache-licensed, PostgreSQL-backed. Multi-warehouse, credential vending for S3/ADLS/GCS, OpenFGA-based fine-grained authorisation, OIDC auth. Light enough for a laptop
Apache Polaris Apache project (originated at Snowflake). Java, REST spec, RBAC with principals/roles/grants, credential vending
Unity Catalog OSS Linux Foundation project (originated at Databricks). Governs tables (Delta and Iceberg via REST), volumes, functions and models
Project Nessie Git-like catalog: branches and commits across many tables
Managed AWS Glue / S3 Tables, Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Open Catalog, Google BigLake metastore — all expose Iceberg REST endpoints

Choose by: which engines you need, whether you need fine-grained auth, where you run (laptop vs managed cloud), and multi-table semantics.

4. Running Lakekeeper locally — step by step

Exact environment variable names and images change between releases; use this as the shape and check the project's quick-start docker-compose for the version you pin.

# compose.yaml
services:
  minio:
    image: minio/minio
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"
    environment: { MINIO_ROOT_USER: admin, MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: password123 }
    ports: ["9000:9000", "9001:9001"]

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment: { POSTGRES_USER: lake, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: lake, POSTGRES_DB: lakekeeper }

  migrate:                                   # one-off: creates the catalog schema in Postgres
    image: quay.io/lakekeeper/catalog:latest
    command: ["migrate"]
    environment: &lk
      LAKEKEEPER__PG_DATABASE_URL_READ:  postgresql://lake:lake@db:5432/lakekeeper
      LAKEKEEPER__PG_DATABASE_URL_WRITE: postgresql://lake:lake@db:5432/lakekeeper
      LAKEKEEPER__PG_ENCRYPTION_KEY: change-me-to-a-long-random-string
    depends_on: [db]

  lakekeeper:
    image: quay.io/lakekeeper/catalog:latest
    command: ["serve"]
    environment: *lk
    ports: ["8181:8181"]
    depends_on: [migrate, minio]

docker compose up -d
mc alias set local http://localhost:9000 admin password123
mc mb local/warehouse

Create a warehouse (a named storage location + credentials) through the management API:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8181/management/v1/warehouse \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
    "warehouse-name": "demo",
    "storage-profile": { "type": "s3", "bucket": "warehouse", "region": "local-01",
                         "endpoint": "http://minio:9000", "path-style-access": true,
                         "flavor": "minio", "sts-enabled": false },
    "storage-credential": { "type": "s3", "credential-type": "access-key",
                            "aws-access-key-id": "admin", "aws-secret-access-key": "password123" }
  }'

Now every engine points at http://localhost:8181/catalog with warehouse demo.

5. Connecting engines to the same catalog

PyIceberg

from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog
cat = load_catalog("lake", type="rest", uri="http://localhost:8181/catalog", warehouse="demo")

Spark

spark-sql \
  --packages org.apache.iceberg:iceberg-spark-runtime-3.5_2.12:<version>,org.apache.iceberg:iceberg-aws-bundle:<version> \
  --conf spark.sql.extensions=org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions \
  --conf spark.sql.catalog.lake=org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog \
  --conf spark.sql.catalog.lake.type=rest \
  --conf spark.sql.catalog.lake.uri=http://localhost:8181/catalog \
  --conf spark.sql.catalog.lake.warehouse=demo

Trino (etc/catalog/lake.properties)

connector.name=iceberg
iceberg.catalog.type=rest
iceberg.rest-catalog.uri=http://lakekeeper:8181/catalog
iceberg.rest-catalog.warehouse=demo

DuckDB — attach the REST catalog with the iceberg extension (chapter 06).

Write with PyIceberg, read with Trino, compact with Spark — one table, one source of truth.

6. Credential vending

---
title: Credential vending flow
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Engine
    participant C as REST catalog
    participant I as Identity provider
    participant S as Object storage
    E->>I: authenticate (OAuth2 client credentials)
    I-->>E: access token
    E->>C: load table silver.nav (bearer token)
    C->>C: check permission: may this principal read silver.nav?
    C->>S: request short-lived credentials scoped to s3://warehouse/silver/nav/
    S-->>C: temporary credentials
    C-->>E: table metadata + temporary credentials
    E->>S: read data files with temporary credentials

Benefits: engines hold no long-lived bucket keys; access is scoped to one table's prefix; revoking catalog permission revokes storage access.

7. Governance in the catalog

  • Namespaces per layer or domain, permissions granted at namespace level, exceptions at table level.
  • Roles, not people: ingest_writer writes Bronze, curation_writer writes Silver, certifier creates tags on Gold, analyst reads Gold.
  • Separate warehouses (or catalogs) for dev/test/prod; never share prod credentials with dev.
  • Audit: catalog logs show who loaded and committed which table, when.

8. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why is the catalog the only component in Iceberg that needs strong consistency?
  2. What happens on the server when two clients send commits with the same assert-ref-snapshot-id?
  3. What does credential vending protect against that bucket policies alone do not?
  4. When would you choose Nessie's multi-table branches over per-table Iceberg branches?
  5. List the configuration Spark needs to talk to a REST catalog.

9. Review checklist

  • One REST catalog shared by all engines; no engine writes by path.
  • Catalog database backed up and monitored.
  • OAuth2 (or equivalent) for engines; credential vending enabled.
  • Permissions by role and namespace; certification rights separated from write rights.
  • Separate warehouses for each environment.
